case_title: Suresh Kumar v. State of Haryana
evidence_type: Oral testimony of prosecution witnesses on dowry demand and cruelty; FIR; statement under s.313 Cr.P.C.; absence of doctor's evidence on cause of death
aggravating_circumstances: Demand for motorcycle as dowry; beating of victim despite intervention; death within seven years of marriage; cruelty about 15 or 20 days before death
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of s.498-A and s.304-B IPC (death held accidental)
high_court_outcome: State's appeal allowed; acquittal reversed; convicted under s.304-B (7 years RI) and s.498-A (3 years RI and fine of Rs.5,000)
offence_finally_established: Dowry death under IPC s.304-B; cruelty under IPC s.498-A
neutral_facts: The victim was married to the accused in February 1990. The accused was serving in the army and stayed at the matrimonial home only while on leave. The prosecution case was that, soon after the marriage, the accused demanded a motorcycle as dowry and threatened that the victim would not be allowed to remain in the matrimonial home if the demand was not met. Relatives of the victim, including her brother and a village companion, intervened and pacified the accused on more than one occasion. In the days before the victim's death in September 1993, the demand was renewed, the accused harassed the victim and beat her. On 16 September 1993 the accused's brother visited the victim's brother's village and reported that the victim had died after suffering an electric shock. When the victim's brother and others reached the matrimonial village, they learned that the body had already been cremated. Enquiries led the victim's brother to conclude that the victim had been killed for dowry by the accused and the accused's mother. A first information report was lodged on 19 September 1993 and the accused was arrested the same day. The evidence consisted of oral testimony from the victim's brother, a village companion, the victim's father and another witness about the dowry demand and the cruelty, and evidence from the village Sarpanch about the cremation. No doctor who allegedly attended the victim was examined and no medical evidence on the cause of death was produced. The electrocution explanation rested on the accused's brother, who did not testify, and the accused did not mention electrocution in his statement under section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
offence_severity: Minimum 7 years; maximum imprisonment for life (IPC s.304-B(2))
physical_harm: Death of victim by alleged electric shock or electrocution, held not a normal circumstance
motive: Demand for a motorcycle as dowry
key_evidence_accepted: Testimony of PW-4 Gian Singh, PW-5 Mam Chand, PW-6 Sardha and PW-7 Beer Singh on dowry demand and cruelty; High Court finding of cruelty about 15 or 20 days before death; death within seven years of marriage
witness_credibility: Trial court discarded Gian Singh's testimony; High Court and Supreme Court accepted prosecution witnesses' evidence on dowry demand and cruelty; the electrocution theory came only from a witness who did not testify
custody_duration: Not stated (arrested on 19 September 1993; duration in custody not given)
bail_history: Bail bond cancelled by Supreme Court; accused directed to be taken into custody to serve remainder of sentence
trial_duration: offence: 16 September 1993 (death); trial judgment: 3 October 1996; High Court: 25 March 2008; Supreme Court: 11 November 2013
legal_representation: Accused: R.C. Kohli, S.S. Shamshery, Bhakti Vardhan. State: Kamal Mohan Gupta, Rajeev Gaur Naseem, Mohd. Zahid Hussain, Naresh Bakshi
investigation_status: FIR registered 19 September 1993; accused arrested; charge-sheeted and tried; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Delay in lodging FIR alleged for first time before Supreme Court; rejected. No other irregularity noted
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted. High Court: acquittal reversed, convicted under s.304-B and s.498-A. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld
defence_argument: Nothing showed guilt under s.304-B; High Court should not have lightly interfered with acquittal; death by electrocution was an accident outside s.304-B; prosecution should have produced the doctor; FIR delay vitiated prosecution
legal_principle_applied: Two-stage process: first ingredients of s.304-B must be proved; then the statutory presumption under s.113-B Evidence Act (mandatory, rebuttable) shifts reverse onus to accused. Accidental death still falls within s.304-B. Appellate interference with acquittal permitted for jurisdictional error
precedent_relied_upon: Pawan Kumar v. State of Haryana (1998) 3 SCC 309; Kans Raj v. State of Punjab (2000) 5 SCC 207; Hira Lal v. State (Govt. of NCT) Delhi (2003) 8 SCC 80; Bakshish Ram v. State of Punjab (2013) 4 SCC 131; Shamnsaheb M. Multtani v. State of Karnataka (2001) 2 SCC 577; Yashoda v. State of MP (2004) 3 SCC 98; Ghurey Lal v. State of UP (2008) 10 SCC 450; Rohtash v. State of Haryana (2012) 6 SCC 589; S. Anil Kumar v. State of Karnataka (2013) 7 SCC 219
other_sentence_order: Bail bond cancelled; accused to be taken into custody to serve remainder of sentence
